(11) Developer Experience (DX) vs. Agent Experience (AX)

Developer (DX) Agent (AX)
Uses the capability Through an application Directly
When Design time Runtime
Use case knowledge Coded into the application, a workflow Found dynamically, best matching tool for now
Context Experience, colleagues, documentation What the tools and their descriptions say


Agents Meet Your APIs Erik Wilde: What AI Agents Are Teaching Us About Integration

(12) Four Places Where Agents Stumble

Where the agent stumbles In the experiment
Discovery The agent does not know what it can do Partly observed
Semantics Descriptions that only make sense with the documentation Not tested
Composition Calls that only get something done when chained Observed
Errors Responses that derail the agent or do not help it recover Partly observed

(16) Two Tasks

Task 1: Find the first issue ever opened in cli/cli, not counting pull requests. Who wrote the first comment on it, and when was that person's GitHub account created?

Task 2: Take the first five issues ever opened in cli/cli, not counting pull requests. For each, count the comments from before 2020 that were written by someone other than the author of the issue. Which issue has the most, and how many?

(22) The Creation Date Is in the OpenAPI Description 

# GitHub OpenAPI description (excerpt)
paths:
  /users/{username}:
    get:
      operationId: users/get-by-username
      summary: Get a user
      responses:
        "200":
          content:
            application/json:
              schema:
                oneOf:
                  - $ref: "#/components/schemas/private-user"
                  - $ref: "#/components/schemas/public-user"
components:
  schemas:
    public-user:
      required: [login, id, ..., created_at, ...]
      properties:
        created_at:
          type: string
          format: date-time

(23) The Generated MCP Tool Returns It 

# MCP tool definition (from tools/list, trimmed, shown as YAML)
# generated from the OpenAPI description, one tool per operation
name: usersget_by_username
description: |
  Provides publicly available information about someone with a GitHub account.

  If the specified user has a [private profile](...), the `followers` and
  `following` values are `0` unless the request is authenticated as that user.
  [...]
inputSchema:
  type: object
  properties:
    username:
      type: string
      description: The handle for the GitHub user account.
  required: [username]
outputSchema:
  properties:
    result:
      anyOf:
        - title: Private User
          # ...
        - title: Public User
          properties:
            login: {type: string}
            id: {type: integer}
            # ...
            created_at: {type: string, format: date-time}
            # ...

# MCP tool definition (from tools/list, trimmed, shown as YAML)
name: search_users
description: >-
  Find GitHub users by username, real name, or other profile information.
  Useful for locating developers, contributors, or team members.
inputSchema:
  type: object
  properties:
    query:
      type: string
      description: >-
        User search query. Examples: 'john smith', 'location:seattle',
        'followers:>100'. Search is automatically scoped to type:user.
    sort:
      type: string
      description: >-
        Sort users by number of followers or repositories, or when the
        person joined GitHub.
      enum: [followers, repositories, joined]
  required: [query]

(27) Some Problems Are Better Answered by Computation, Not Inference

CPU Computation LLM Inference
Elapsed time a few nanoseconds ~0.1–2 seconds
Computation one integer division ~1011–1013 FLOPs
Energy ~pJ–nJ ~1–100 J
Correctness exact not guaranteed
  • CPU: One deterministic instruction
  • LLM: Trillions of operations for probabilistic inference
  • The LLM might still get the answer wrong


As Little AI As Possible Erik Wilde: What AI Agents Are Teaching Us About Integration

(30) Which Corner of the Garden Should You Focus on First?

  • Where are you? How many APIs, how much pressure?
  • What failures do you see? Exposure or what you expose?
  • How big is your landscape going to be?
  • What is on leadership's radar?


Architect for Change Erik Wilde: What AI Agents Are Teaching Us About Integration

(31) A Starting Point: Five Techniques

Technique Effort What you get
Check your APIs for AI readiness Easy Awareness, helps going forward
Improve the descriptions Cheap, can be automated A bit better
Improve the API designs Varies, needs the API teams Better results, more effort
Select or search the tools Select by hand, search, or both Not everything in the context
Orchestrate tools into AI-friendly designs Higher (Arazzo or other ways) High payback if it is easy to do

(34) What Agents Are Teaching Us

  • Integration problems did not go away, they moved from design time to runtime
  • Watch your agents, and look into the traces
  • Which parts need the runtime creativity of agents, which are fine with workflows? Architect so you can play with that line


Conclusions Erik Wilde: What AI Agents Are Teaching Us About Integration

(35) Monday Tasks

  • Point an agent at one of your APIs and look into the traces
  • When it engineers around a missing tool, give it the tool
  • Start with the corner of the garden that leadership is pushing
